---
title: "Creating documents with Quarto"
---

Quarto lets you create professional reports and papers directly from RStudio, combining code, text, and visualizations in a single reproducible workflow. This tutorial covers the basics of working with Quarto files in RStudio, then walks through creating report-style documents specifically. The next tutorial covers presentations.

## Working with Quarto in RStudio

To start a new Quarto document in RStudio:

1. Go to **File → New File → Quarto Document...**
2. Enter a **title**, **author**, and choose a **default output format** (e.g., HTML, PDF, or Word).
3. RStudio creates a `.qmd` file containing a template YAML header and an example code chunk.
4. Click **Render** (or use *Render on Save*) to produce the formatted output.

![RStudio Quarto new document dialog (source: https://quarto.org)](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/authoring/images/rstudio-new-document.png)

::: reading
For more information, see the official Quarto documentation: [Authoring with RStudio](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/authoring/rstudio.html)
:::

Every `.qmd` file has the same basic structure: a **YAML header** (between `---` lines) defining metadata like title
and output format, a **body** written in Markdown, and optional embedded R code chunks.

## YAML: Document Metadata and Configuration

The YAML header is where you tell Quarto *how* to render your document: what format to produce and which options to
apply. It uses a simple key-value structure, enclosed between `---` at the start and end of the block.

```yaml
---
title: "Statistical Analysis of Air Quality Data"
author: "Alex Rivera"
date: "2025-01-01"
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    code-fold: true
---
```

**Do:** Create a Quarto document on your own computer. In the YAML header of the `.qmd` file, change `format: html` to `format: pdf` in the header. Do you expect this to be a one-line switch, or would you need to change other parts of the document too?

**See:** For a simple document, changing the target format really can be that simple: the same Markdown body and
code chunks are reused. In practice, though, some format-specific options (like `code-fold`, which is an HTML-only
feature) won't carry over, and PDF output has its own setup requirements, covered below.

## Creating Reports and Papers

Common document output formats include:

| **Format** | **Output Type**        | **Typical Use**                        |
|------------|------------------------|-----------------------------------------|
| `html`     | Interactive web report | Exploratory data reports, dashboards   |
| `pdf`      | Print-quality report   | Academic papers, formatted submissions |
| `docx`     | Microsoft Word         | Editable reports for collaboration     |
| `epub`     | e-book                 | Long-form reading materials            |

Quarto automatically executes embedded code chunks and inserts the resulting tables and plots, so every time you
re-render, the analysis and visuals update from your current data.

A few things to keep in mind across formats:

- **Layout:** reports may need page breaks or fixed figure sizing, especially for PDF and Word.
- **PDF rendering** requires a working LaTeX installation (e.g., TinyTeX).
- **Settings don't always transfer:** an option that works for HTML may not apply to PDF or Word.
- **Citations** are supported via BibTeX, covered later in this module.

::: {.callout-note}
## Common Mistake

By default, a rendered HTML report can reference supporting files, such as separately saved images, rather than
embedding everything into the single `.html` file. If you then hand in or share only that `.html` file, without its supporting files, it can open broken or missing content for whoever receives it. To avoid this, set your document to be **self-contained** by adding `embed-resources: true` under your HTML format options:

```yaml
format:
  html:
    embed-resources: true
```

This produces a single, fully portable `.html` file with everything, including plots and images, embedded inside it. This is important whenever you're submitting a report as one file, for example for a homework assignment.
:::

## Practice Exercise

:::: {.panel-tabset}
## {{< var tab_title.question >}}

Write a YAML header for an HTML report titled "Analysis Report," with a table of contents, that is safe to hand in as a single file.

## {{< var tab_title.solution >}}

```yaml
---
title: "Analysis Report"
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    embed-resources: true
---
```

The `toc: true` option adds a table of contents, and `embed-resources: true` ensures the rendered `.html` file is
self-contained, so it can be shared or submitted on its own.
